headline: High risk: gpt-engineer can write and execute code in a shared project directory while emqx has broad network egress, creating dangerous default pathways for leakage and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No direct shared channel is documented, but gpt-engineer writes files in a user project directory and can later run them, while emqx exposes an HTTP API and broad network egress. That makes manual file-based prompt injection plausible if outputs are copied between them. The pathway is weaker than default shared-memory bridges, so low fits.
conditions: IF the operator copies emqx-generated text into gpt-engineer project files
IF gpt-engineer is instructed to execute or parse those files as prompts
mitigations: Keep the agents in separate directories
Do not paste broker output into code prompts
Add a human review step before any file is treated as instructions
Use a read-only export format for emqx outputs
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to files

B_data_leakage.rationale: gpt-engineer reads and writes the project directory and sends prompts to a configured model; emqx handles IoT data and has broad network egress. If IoT data is placed in the shared workspace, gpt-engineer can ingest it and transmit it to a third-party model backend. The pairwise leakage path exists in default workflows, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF IoT data is stored in the project directory
IF gpt-engineer forwards that directory content into model prompts
mitigations: Keep IoT data out of the coding workspace
Redact secrets before prompting gpt-engineer
Use a local model for gpt-engineer
Restrict project directory permissions
requires-engineering: separate data and code workspaces

C_capability_conflict.rationale: emqx has broad network egress and HTTP API access, while gpt-engineer can execute shell commands, install packages, read and write the filesystem, and spawn subprocesses in a per-project session. Their overlapping mutable surfaces create a realistic conflict over the same project directory or downstream resources, even though gpt-engineer does not modify git state. Uncertainty favors medium.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same project directory
IF emqx-triggered artifacts are consumed while gpt-engineer is writing files
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Serialize access with a lock file
Disable shell execution in gpt-engineer sessions
Run emqx and gpt-engineer under separate OS users
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: gpt-engineer can write files and execute generated code, and its tool-use pattern is to write files then offer to run them. If emqx output is treated as authoritative input, errors can cascade into code generation and execution with user privileges. That creates an irreversible blast radius beyond simple misformatting, so high is appropriate.
conditions: IF emqx output is fed into gpt-engineer as trusted requirements
IF gpt-engineer is allowed to run generated code
mitigations: Require human verification of emqx-derived facts
Disable automatic execution of generated code
Use test-only runs before any real action
Limit generated code to a sandbox
requires-engineering: add schema validation for upstream outputs

E_compliance.rationale: emqx touches IoT data, while gpt-engineer handles generated source code and stores an OPENAI_API_KEY. The profiles do not document a residency mismatch, but they do show different data classes and retention-sensitive artifacts flowing through a third-party model backend. Because compliance gaps are plausible but not explicit, medium is the cautious choice.
conditions: IF IoT data includes regulated personal data
IF that data is sent through gpt-engineer to an external model provider
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from prompts
Document data handling boundaries
Rotate any exposed API keys
Use a local inference backend
requires-engineering: add residency and retention controls
